packages and ships stuff out of the cell. like a post office

All correct. You clearly know this — anything you actually want me to check rather than just confirm?

missed bio monday. whats the actual difference between mitosis and meiosis, i keep mixing them up
What's your current understanding — even if you think it's wrong, tell me what you've got.
i think mitosis makes 2 cells and meiosis makes 4? and one of them is for sex cells
That's mostly right. Which one is for sex cells?
meiosis. thats the 4 one
Correct. So why does meiosis need to make 4 instead of 2 — what's it for that mitosis isn't?
growing/repairing vs making eggs and sperm. so meiosis has to cut the chromosome number in half so when they combine it goes back to normal
That's the actual reason, yes. So if a human cell has 46 chromosomes, what does each cell coming out of meiosis have?
23. so when sperm and egg combine its 46 again
That's it. You had the right pieces, you just hadn't connected why meiosis has to halve the number. Anything else from Monday you're missing?
no i think i got it now, that was the confusing part
can you explain again the thing about angles from friday, i missed it
Which part — do you know what topic it was?
something about angles when two lines cross another line. transversal i think
Yes, transversals. When a transversal crosses two parallel lines, it creates pairs of angles with specific relationships. Do you know any of the angle pair names already?
alternate interior angles are equal i remember that much
Right. What about corresponding angles — where are those positioned relative to each other?
same corner but on different lines? so like top left on both
Exactly, same position at each intersection. And what's true about their measures?
equal too i think
Correct. One more — co-interior, also called same-side interior. Any guess what's true about those, given the other two are both equal?
if the other ones are equal maybe these add up to something instead. 180?
That's right, they're supplementary. You reconstructed that one yourself. Want to try a problem using all three?
yeah give me one
A transversal crosses two parallel lines. One of the angles formed measures 65°. Find the corresponding angle, the alternate interior angle, and the co-interior angle at the other intersection.
corresponding would be 65, alternate interior would also be 65, and co-interior would be 115 since 180-65
All three correct.

the idea that colonies exist to make money for the home country

the trade route between europe, africa, and the americas. slaves, goods, raw materials

what did geometry cover today, im not going to be there
Today was similar triangles — how to prove two triangles are similar and how to use that to find missing sides. Want the short version or should I walk you through an example?
short version first then an example

Short version: if two triangles have two matching angles (AA), or all three sides in the same ratio (SSS), or two sides in ratio with the matching angle between them (SAS), they're similar. Similar means same shape, scaled size — so their sides are proportional.
ok wait so if theyre similar i can set up a ratio between the sides and solve for the missing one
Yes. Here's an example: triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF. AB=6, DE=9, BC=8. Find EF.
so 6/9 = 8/EF. cross multiply, 6EF = 72, EF = 12
Correct. Why did you set the ratio up as 6/9 instead of 9/6?
bc AB matches to DE and BC matches to EF so i just kept the order the same on both sides
Right, keeping corresponding sides in the same position is exactly what matters there. That's the whole lesson, basically — you're ready.
aight good, saves me asking someone tomorrow

can u check this proof. trying to show these two triangles are congruent. i used SAS. Given: AB = DE, angle B = angle E, BC = EF. Prove: triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF. Statement: AB=DE (given), angle B = angle E (given), BC=EF (given), therefore triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF by SAS.
Walk me through why those three pieces are enough — why doesn't SSA work the same way?
bc if the angle isnt between the two sides the triangle could still be two different shapes even with the same two sides and angle. like it doesnt lock the shape

That's exactly the reason SSA isn't a valid congruence rule. Your proof itself is correct — SAS with the angle between the two given sides is valid. One thing missing: you need to state the angle is between the two sides explicitly, or it's ambiguous which theorem applies.
oh right lemme add that. angle B is included between side AB and side BC, same for E
That's a complete proof now.

That's actually the key detail historians argue about — good instinct to hold onto that. Here's the rest: on April 19, 1775, British troops marched to seize colonial weapons stores near Concord. Given who wrote each, what would you expect each one to emphasize, even if both are describing the same real event?
the factory one would prob blame the workers and the union one would blame the factory or the cops
Right. So neither is neutral. Does that mean you can't use either one?
no i think you can still use both, you just gotta say why each one might be slanted. like use the newspaper for what actually happened logistically but not for who to blame

Okay — Section 4 answers: the Stamp Act taxed printed materials and was repealed after colonial boycotts; the Townshend Acts taxed imported goods like glass and tea and led to the Boston Massacre; the Boston Tea Party was a protest against the Tea Act where colonists dumped tea into the harbor. we got a lab practical coming up on genetics, punnett squares and stuff. i wanna practice without looking at my notes first to see what i actually remember
Good plan. Here's a cross: heterozygous brown eyes (Bb) x heterozygous brown eyes (Bb), brown is dominant. What's the genotype ratio of the offspring?
1 BB, 2 Bb, 1 bb
Right. Phenotype ratio?
3 brown to 1 blue
Correct. Now a trickier one — incomplete dominance, red flower (RR) x white flower (WW), and the heterozygote is pink. Cross two pink flowers, what's the phenotype ratio?
wait if theyre pink thats Rr right, so Rr x Rr... 1 RR red, 2 Rr pink, 1 WW — wait no there is no WW in incomplete dominance thats codominance im mixing them up

Good catch stopping yourself — you're right that WW doesn't reappear the same way. In incomplete dominance there's no W allele at all, just R and a different allele, call it R'. Rr is really RR' here. Want to redo it with that fixed?
yeah so RR' x RR' — 1 RR red, 2 RR' pink, 1 R'R' white. 1:2:1 phenotype same as genotype since none of them are fully dominant
That's exactly right, and you fixed your own mistake mid-answer, which is the actual skill for the practical.

Given: AB is parallel to CD, and AD is parallel to BC (quadrilateral ABCD). Prove: ABCD is a parallelogram. Statement: AB || CD (given), AD || BC (given), therefore ABCD is a parallelogram because both pairs of opposite sides are parallel.
Walk me through your logic for the last step — you conclude it's a parallelogram, but what's the actual definition you're using to get there?
a parallelogram is defined as a quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel, so once i show both pairs are parallel im done by definition
That's correct and it's the cleanest way to close a proof like this — straight from the definition instead of a longer theorem. Proof holds.

That's a real structural connection — using independent lines of evidence to converge on one conclusion, whether it's angle relationships or historical sources. That's a pattern that shows up way outside both of those classes too, in things like science experiments needing replication. Where else do you think you'd see it?
